title: Inheritance

items.title: What Is Inheritance?
items.content: Inheritance is a core principle of object-oriented programming that allows a new class to reuse, extend, and modify the behavior of an existing class. The existing class is called the parent (or base) class, and the new class is called the child (or derived) class. In Python, you create a child class by placing the parent class name in parentheses after the child class name. This lets the child class automatically gain the attributes and methods of the parent class without rewriting them. Inheritance promotes code reuse and establishes a natural hierarchy between related concepts. For example, if you have a class Animal with a method speak(), a class Dog can inherit from Animal and reuse that method while adding its own bark() method.
items.explanation: Inheritance is a core principle of object-oriented programming that allows a new class to reuse, extend, and modify the behavior of an existing class. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes inheritance in Python?
options: A child class must always redefine every method from the parent class.
A child class can automatically use the attributes and methods of a parent class.
Inheritance only works when both classes are defined in the same file.
A parent class is created by placing the child class name in parentheses.
items.correct_answer: A child class can automatically use the attributes and methods of a parent class.
items.explanation: Inheritance enables code reuse: the child class gains the parent's attributes and methods. It does not need to redefine them, and the parent class is not defined with the child in parentheses. Inheritance is not restricted by file location.

items.title: Inheritance Syntax in Python
items.explanation: To declare inheritance in Python, write the child class name followed by a parent class name in parentheses. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Match the following class relationships to their correct Python inheritance expressions.
options: Dog inherits from Animal: class Dog(Animal):
Animal inherits from Dog: class Animal(Dog):
Dog inherits from Animal: class Animal(Dog):
Animal inherits from Dog: class Dog(Animal):
items.correct_answer: Dog inherits from Animal: class Dog(Animal):
items.explanation: The child class is listed first, and the parent class is listed in parentheses. Therefore, Dog, the child, inherits from Animal, the parent. The other options either reverse the relationship or use incorrect syntax.

items.prompt: What is a common pitfall when using inheritance in Python?
options: Child classes cannot access parent methods unless they are copied manually.
Overriding a parent method in a child class can lead to unexpected behavior if the override does not call the parent's version when needed.
Inheritance only works if the parent class has no parameters in its constructor.
Multiple inheritance always causes a NameError in Python.
items.correct_answer: Overriding a parent method in a child class can lead to unexpected behavior if the override does not call the parent's version when needed.
items.explanation: A frequent issue is method overriding: the child class replaces the parent method, but sometimes the child needs the original behavior too. Using super() helps avoid this pitfall. The other options are incorrect: parent methods are accessible automatically, constructors can accept parameters, and multiple inheritance is supported though it requires care.

micro_lesson.title: Understanding super() and Method Resolution Order
micro_lesson.content: When a child class overrides a parent method, it can still call the parent's version using super(). The method resolution order (MRO) determines which method gets executed first. If the child does not override a method, the parent's version is used automatically.

items.explanation: The Car class overrides move and calls super().move(), which returns 'Moving'. Concatenating ' fast' yields 'Moving fast'. The super() keyword accesses the parent class method.

micro_lesson.title: Tracing Inheritance Flow with Multiple Levels
micro_lesson.content: Inheritance can span multiple levels. A grandchild class inherits from a child class, which in turn inherits from a parent. When a method is called, Python searches the class hierarchy from the most derived class upward until it finds a matching method.

items.explanation: Class C does not define show, so Python looks in its parent B, which defines show and returns 'B'. The method from A is skipped because B already provides an override.

micro_lesson.title: Logic of Inheritance and Attribute Access
micro_lesson.content: Inheritance also affects attribute access. If an attribute is not found in the child class, Python searches the parent class. However, if the child defines the attribute, it shadows the parent's attribute. Method calls follow the same lookup rules as attributes.

items.explanation: The Child class defines its own value attribute, so c.value returns 20. The Child class also overrides get, so c.get() returns 'Child'. Both lookups resolve in the Child class without falling back to Parent.

micro_lesson.title: Defining a Child Class with Inheritance
micro_lesson.content:
Inheritance allows a new class (child or derived class) to reuse attributes and methods from an existing class (parent or base class). To declare a child class, place the parent class name in parentheses after the child class name. This creates an is-a relationship. For example, a Car class can inherit from a Vehicle class. The syntax is straightforward: the child class header includes the parent class name in parentheses. When you create an instance of the child class, Python automatically looks up the method resolution order (MRO) to find methods. If a method is not defined in the child class, Python searches the parent class. Here is a code example:

```python
class Animal:
    def speak(self):
        return 'Some sound'

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

d = Dog()
print(d.speak())
```

In this example, Dog inherits from Animal. The Dog class does not define speak(), so it uses Animal.speak().

micro_lesson.title: Diagnosing Inheritance Errors
micro_lesson.content: Inheritance errors often arise from incorrect method resolution order (MRO), missing super() calls, or improper attribute access. When a child class does not properly initialize parent attributes, or when methods are overridden without using the parent implementation, runtime errors occur. Common mistakes include calling undefined methods, incorrect constructor chaining, and diamond problem ambiguities. Always verify that super().__init__() is invoked in the child constructor, and trace attribute lookups through the MRO using Class.__mro__.

micro_lesson.title: Runtime Inheritance Errors
micro_lesson.content: Runtime inheritance errors manifest when the program executes but encounters unexpected behavior due to inheritance structure. These include AttributeError when a subclass method expects an attribute not initialized by the parent, TypeError when super() is called incorrectly, and infinite recursion if a method calls itself without base-class delegation. To diagnose, print the MRO with Class.__mro__, inspect instance dictionaries with vars(instance), and verify that every overridden method either delegates to super() or explicitly replicates required logic. Use traceback output to pinpoint the exact line where the exception propagates.

items.prompt: Refactor the following deeply nested inheritance hierarchy to reduce duplication, eliminate redundant attribute assignments, and improve maintainability while preserving all original behavior.
items.starter_code:
class Vehicle:
    def __init__(self, make, model, year):
        self.make = make
        self.model = model
        self.year = year
        self.is_running = False

class Car(Vehicle):
    def __init__(self, make, model, year, num_doors):
        self.make = make
        self.model = model
        self.year = year
        self.num_doors = num_doors
        self.is_running = False

class Truck(Vehicle):
    def __init__(self, make, model, year, payload_capacity):
        self.make = make
        self.model = model
        self.year = year
        self.payload_capacity = payload_capacity
        self.is_running = False

class SportsCar(Car):
    def __init__(self, make, model, year, num_doors, top_speed):
        self.make = make
        self.model = model
        self.year = year
        self.num_doors = num_doors
        self.top_speed = top_speed
        self.is_running = False

def main():
    v = Vehicle('Honda', 'Civic', 2020)
    c = Car('Ford', 'F-150', 2021, 4)
    t = Truck('Chevy', 'Silverado', 2022, 3000)
    s = SportsCar('Porsche', '911', 2023, 2, 190)
    print(v.make, c.num_doors, t.payload_capacity, s.top_speed)

test_cases.description: Verifies: v = Vehicle('Honda', 'Civic', 2020); assert v.make == 'Honda' and v.is_running == False
Verifies: c = Car('Ford', 'F-150', 2021, 4); assert c.num_doors == 4 and isinstance(c, Vehicle)
Verifies: s = SportsCar('Porsche', '911', 2023, 2, 190); assert s.top_speed == 190 and s.num_doors == 2

items.hint: Remove duplicated attribute assignments by calling super().__init__() in each subclass. Ensure SportsCar correctly inherits from Car.
items.explanation: The refactored version eliminates redundant assignments of make, model, year, and is_running in every subclass by delegating to the parent constructor via super().__init__(). SportsCar now inherits from Car and only adds top_speed, preserving all original behavior while reducing code duplication and improving maintainability.
